subsection: 6. War and revolution in Germany, and the Peace Settlement, 1918–1920

notes.h: Germany in 1918: the background to defeat
notes.b: To understand the revolution and the peace, you first need to know who was fighting, why Germany was losing, and how Germany was governed. The old system collapsed because it had been built around a war that was now lost.
points: The war was fought between the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria) and the Allies (Britain, France, Russia until 1917, Italy from 1915 and the USA from 6 April 1917).

By 1918 Germany was losing. Russia had left the war by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918), but the German spring offensive from March failed, and Allied counter-attacks began at Amiens on 8 August, which Ludendorff called the 'black day of the German army'.

American troops were arriving in large numbers, so Germany could not replace its losses. At home the British naval blockade had caused food shortages throughout the war, including the 'turnip winter' of 1916-17, so civilians were exhausted and hungry.

In the Kaiserreich (the German Empire) the Chancellor answered to the Kaiser, not to the Reichstag (the elected parliament). From 1916 the army leaders Hindenburg (Chief of the General Staff) and Ludendorff (First Quartermaster General) dominated government, so the army's failure discredited the whole system.

German socialism had split. The Majority SPD (Social Democratic Party; Ebert and Scheidemann) had backed the war; the Independent Social Democrats (USPD) broke away in April 1917; the Spartacists on the far left (Luxemburg and Liebknecht) wanted revolution.
Austria-Hungary was a multinational empire, and by 1918 its Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, South Slavs, Romanians and others increasingly wanted independence, which weakened it as the war went badly.
notes.tip: Examiners reward cause-and-result chains, so be ready to start the story of 1918 from defeat in the field and the exhausted home front, not from the mutiny.

notes.h: The collapse of the Central Powers, September-October 1918
notes.b: Germany's allies gave way one by one in autumn 1918, and the German army leaders then admitted they could not go on. This pushed Germany into asking for an armistice (an agreement to stop fighting) and into political change.
points: Bulgaria signed an armistice at Salonika on 29 September 1918. The Ottoman Empire followed with the armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918, so Germany lost two allies in a month.

On 29 September 1918, at army headquarters in Spa, Ludendorff told the Kaiser and the government that Germany must seek an armistice at once. Allied attacks had broken into the Hindenburg Line (the main German defensive position in France) and Bulgaria had given up.
To please Wilson, the Kaiser appointed the liberal Prince Max of Baden as Chancellor on 3 October 1918. His government included Social Democrats (Scheidemann) and Centre Party members (Erzberger).
On the night of 3-4 October Germany asked Wilson for an armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points.

Wilson's replies insisted that Germany must end its military autocracy (rule by the army and Kaiser), which encouraged calls for the Kaiser to go. The constitution was changed in late October (28 October) to make the Chancellor responsible to the Reichstag.
Ludendorff resigned on 26 October 1918, so the man who had demanded the armistice was gone before it was signed.

Austria-Hungary was defeated by Italy at the battle of Vittorio Veneto (late October to early November 1918) and signed the armistice of Villa Giusti on 3 November 1918, which came into force on 4 November.
notes.tip: Link the steps in order: Ludendorff's demand, the request to Wilson, Wilson's demand for an end to military autocracy, the reforms, and then the mutiny. That chain is what scores.

notes.b: Defeat turned into revolution within a fortnight. A naval order sparked a mutiny, the mutiny spread, and by 9 November the Kaiser's rule had ended and two rival republics had been proclaimed in Berlin.
points: At the end of October the naval command ordered the High Seas Fleet to sail for a last battle. Sailors at Wilhelmshaven refused.
A mutiny at Kiel, from 3 November, spread within days to ports and cities across Germany. The SPD sent Gustav Noske to Kiel on 4 November to regain control.

Sailors, soldiers and workers formed councils on the Russian model, local bodies that took over authority from the old officials. Kurt Eisner (USPD) declared a Bavarian republic in Munich on 7 November.
On 9 November, with a general strike and crowds in Berlin, Prince Max announced the Kaiser's abdication without his consent and handed the chancellorship to the Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert.

Two republics were proclaimed that day. Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a parliamentary German republic from a window of the Reichstag, and Karl Liebknecht later proclaimed a 'free socialist republic' from the Berlin palace.
Wilhelm II crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November and signed a formal abdication on 28 November. He lived there until his death in 1941.

The armistice was signed at about 5 am on 11 November 1918 in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne, in force at 11 am. Matthias Erzberger of the Centre Party led the German delegation; Marshal Foch signed for the Allies.

Its terms: evacuate occupied France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine; hand over large amounts of weapons, the submarines and much of the fleet; Allied occupation west of the Rhine with bridgeheads; Brest-Litovsk cancelled; blockade kept on until July 1919.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the two 9 November republics: Scheidemann's was parliamentary and spoke from the Reichstag, Liebknecht's was socialist and spoke from the palace. Also keep the armistice (11 November 1918) separate from the Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919).

notes.h: The provisional government and the choice facing Germany
notes.b: With the Kaiser gone, someone had to run Germany. Ebert's government had to decide whether to build a new order from the revolution or to keep the old institutions working, and its choices shaped the republic's weaknesses.
points: The Council of People's Representatives, the provisional government set up on 10 November 1918, had three Majority SPD members (including Ebert and Scheidemann) and three USPD members. It ruled until elections; the USPD members resigned on 29 December 1918.
Do not confuse it with the workers' and soldiers' councils, which were local bodies formed during the revolution.
The Ebert-Groener pact, made by telephone on 10 November: General Groener (Ludendorff's successor) pledged the army's support against Bolshevism, and Ebert's government respected officers' authority.

The pact helped the republic survive, because the army would defend order against the far left. It was also a weakness, because it left the old army, civil service and judiciary in place, still loyal to the old order rather than the republic.

The Stinnes-Legien agreement of 15 November 1918 was made between the industrialist Hugo Stinnes and the trade union leader Carl Legien. Employers recognised the unions and accepted the eight-hour day, which won workers' cooperation and helped to block revolution.
The central choice was between a council republic on the Russian model, which the far left wanted, and an elected parliament, which the SPD leaders wanted.
notes.tip: Explain the Ebert-Groener pact as both the republic's survival and its weakness; examiners look for both sides.

notes.h: The Spartacist rising and the murder of the left's leaders
notes.b: The split on the left turned violent in January 1919. The government used the army and volunteer units to crush the radicals, and this left a lasting bitterness on the left.
points: The KPD (Communist Party of Germany) was founded at a congress from 30 December 1918 to 1 January 1919 by the Spartacus League and other left-radical groups. They wanted a council republic like Russia's.
The trigger for the rising was the dismissal on 4 January 1919 of Emil Eichhorn, the USPD police chief of Berlin, whom the left saw as a defender of the revolution.
In the Spartacist or January rising (5-12 January 1919) radicals occupied newspaper buildings in Berlin, including the SPD paper Vorwärts.
It was crushed by government troops and Freikorps (volunteer units of ex-soldiers) under Gustav Noske, the SPD member of the government in charge of military affairs.
Luxemburg and Liebknecht were arrested and murdered by Freikorps officers in Berlin on 15 January 1919, so the KPD lost its leaders at once.
Eisner was assassinated on 21 February 1919. A Bavarian Soviet republic existed in Munich in April 1919 and was crushed by government troops and Freikorps in early May 1919.
notes.tip: On the Spartacist rising, give the trigger, the KPD's founding, how it was crushed, the murders and their lasting effect on the left. Keep Eisner's Bavarian republic of November 1918 separate from the Soviet republic of April 1919.

notes.b: Once the left was beaten, the SPD could hold elections and write a constitution. The republic was democratic, but it started with heavy handicaps.
points: In the National Assembly election of 19 January 1919 women voted nationally for the first time (votes for men and women over 20). The SPD was the largest party with about 38 per cent. The Weimar coalition was the SPD, the Catholic Centre Party and the German Democratic Party (DDP).
The Assembly first met at Weimar on 6 February 1919, away from Berlin's unrest. Ebert was elected Reich President on 11 February, and Scheidemann became head of the first government.

The Weimar constitution was passed by the Assembly on 31 July 1919 and signed by Ebert on 11 August. The president was elected for seven years, there was proportional representation, and Article 48 gave emergency powers.

The 'stab in the back' (Dolchstoss) myth claimed that the army had not been beaten in the field but betrayed by socialists, Jews and revolutionaries at home. It was false, because the army leaders themselves had asked for an armistice. Hindenburg repeated it to a Reichstag committee in November 1919.
Nationalists called the politicians who accepted the armistice and the republic the 'November criminals', so the republic was tied in people's minds to defeat.
The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 showed the right's hostility: Wolfgang Kapp and Freikorps units seized Berlin and the army did not resist them. It was defeated within days by a general strike.
notes.tip: When asked about the 'stab in the back', say why it was false: the army leaders had themselves demanded the armistice.

notes.b: While Germany had a revolution, the Habsburg empire simply fell apart along national lines. It broke up in October and November 1918, before the peace treaties, and the treaties then confirmed what had happened.
points: Emperor Charles I issued a manifesto on 16 October 1918 offering to turn Austria into a federation of nationalities. It came too late, because the peoples now wanted independence.

Czechoslovakia declared independence in Prague on 28 October 1918, with Tomas Masaryk as its first president. A State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs was declared on 29 October, and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia) was proclaimed on 1 December.
Poland declared independence in November 1918 (11 November is its independence day; Jozef Pilsudski was its leader), and Hungary became a separate state.
Charles withdrew from state affairs in Austria on 11 November 1918. German-Austria proclaimed a republic on 12 November, and its assembly declared it part of the German republic.

Hungary was in turmoil. Bela Kun's Hungarian Soviet Republic (March to August 1919) ended after a Romanian invasion, when Romanian troops entered Budapest. Admiral Horthy then took power and became regent in 1920.

notes.h: Wilson's Fourteen Points and the armistice agreement
notes.b: The Fourteen Points were Wilson's programme for a just peace. Germany asked for an armistice on their basis, so what they promised mattered when the Germans saw the treaty.
points: Wilson set out the Fourteen Points in an address to Congress on 8 January 1918, as a statement of American war aims and a basis for peace. It was partly a reply to the Bolsheviks, who had published the Allies' secret treaties and called for peace.

Points 1 to 5 called for open covenants (public agreements) of peace openly arrived at, freedom of the seas, removal of economic barriers (free trade), reduction of armaments, and an impartial adjustment of colonial claims in which the interests of the peoples concerned counted equally.
Points 6 to 8 dealt with the evacuation of Russia and Belgium and the return of Alsace-Lorraine to France.

Points 9 to 13 set Italy's frontiers on lines of nationality, called for autonomous development for the peoples of Austria-Hungary, and covered the Balkans and the Ottoman Empire (Turkish parts sovereign, others autonomous, the Dardanelles open). They also demanded an independent Poland with access to the sea.
Point 10 asked for 'autonomous development', not independence, for the peoples of Austria-Hungary. By 1918 Wilson came to back independence for the Czechoslovaks and South Slavs.

Point 14 called for a general association of nations to guarantee independence and territorial integrity (the right of a state to keep its borders) to great and small states alike. This became the League of Nations.

In the pre-armistice agreement (the Lansing note, 5 November 1918) the Allies accepted the Points as the basis of peace. Britain reserved its position on freedom of the seas, and the Allies demanded compensation for damage done to the civilian population.
Many Germans later believed that the harsher Treaty of Versailles broke this agreement.
notes.tip: Do not say the Fourteen Points used the word 'self-determination'. They proposed frontiers along lines of nationality and autonomous development; Wilson used the phrase in speeches later in 1918. Exams on Wilson ask what Point 14 proposed.

notes.h: The Paris Peace Conference: organisation and the main aims
notes.b: The conference opened in Paris on 18 January 1919, the anniversary of the German Empire's proclamation in 1871. About thirty states took part, but the leaders of four of them took the decisions, and each had a different aim.
points: The defeated powers were excluded and Soviet Russia was not invited. A Council of Ten (two leading delegates each from the USA, Britain, France, Italy and Japan) took decisions at first, then the Council of Four (the Big Four) from March 1919. Commissions drafted the terms.
The Big Four were Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France) and Vittorio Orlando (Italy).

Wilson wanted a just peace based on self-determination, with the League built into the treaty. He arrived in France on 13 December 1918 and was the first US president to travel to Europe while in office.
Clemenceau, French Prime Minister, nicknamed 'the Tiger', wanted security for France, which had been invaded in 1870 and 1914. He wanted a weak Germany, a Rhineland buffer and heavy reparations.
France at first wanted the Rhineland separated from Germany. It accepted occupation and demilitarisation of the Rhineland in return for a promised Anglo-American guarantee of French security.

Lloyd George, British Prime Minister, had won the general election of 14 December 1918 amid popular demands to make Germany pay and to try the Kaiser. He nevertheless wanted a peace that would not provoke revenge.

His Fontainebleau memorandum (25 March 1919) warned against a peace that would drive Germany to revenge or Bolshevism. He also wanted to protect British trade, empire and naval power, and to avoid French dominance in Europe.
notes.tip: Exams ask for each leader's aim and the exclusion of the defeated. Explaining why Germans resented the treaty earns more than listing terms, so tie each leader's aim to what appeared in the treaty.

notes.h: Other claims at Paris and the handing over of the terms
notes.b: Other states came to Paris with claims of their own, and most were disappointed. The Germans were given no chance to negotiate, which shaped how they saw the result.
points: Orlando wanted what the secret Treaty of London (April 1915) had promised Italy to bring it into the war: South Tyrol (Trentino to the Brenner), Trieste, Istria and much of Dalmatia. Fiume was not among the promises, but Italy claimed it as well.
Orlando left the conference in April 1919 over Fiume and returned in May. Italian nationalists, including Gabriele d'Annunzio, spoke of a 'mutilated victory'.
Japan, an ally, proposed a racial equality clause, which was rejected in April 1919. It received Germany's rights in Shandong (China).
Ireland's Sinn Fein sent Seán T. O'Kelly as Dáil Éireann's envoy to Paris in 1919 to ask for a hearing for Irish self-determination. Wilson and the Allies refused to admit the Irish case.
The terms were presented on 7 May 1919 to the German delegation, led by Foreign Minister Ulrich von Brockdorff-Rantzau. There was no negotiation: German counter-proposals were mostly rejected.
In June 1919 the Allies issued an ultimatum to sign or face renewed war, so Germany had no real choice.
notes.tip: Do not write that Fiume was promised in 1915; the Treaty of London did not include it. Say Italy claimed Fiume in addition to the 1915 promises.

notes.h: The Treaty of Versailles: signing, war guilt and territory
notes.b: The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination at Sarajevo. The Hall of Mirrors was also where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871, so the setting was deliberate.
points: Article 231, the war guilt clause, said that Germany accepted responsibility for itself and its allies for causing all the loss and damage suffered by the Allies in a war imposed on them by the aggression of Germany and its allies. It was the legal basis for reparations.
The word 'guilt' does not appear in Article 231; Germans called it the war guilt clause because they read it as blaming Germany alone.
In the west and north, Alsace-Lorraine went to France, Eupen and Malmedy to Belgium, and North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite (a vote on a border) in 1920.

In the east, most of West Prussia and Posen went to Poland, forming the Polish Corridor to the Baltic, which separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Plebiscites were held in Upper Silesia and in East Prussian districts.
Danzig became a Free City under League of Nations protection, so it was neither German nor Polish, and Memel was placed under Allied control (Lithuania seized it in 1923).
The Saar was governed by the League for fifteen years, its coal mines went to France, and a plebiscite was due in 1935.
Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory and about a tenth of its population, which is why many Germans saw the treaty as national humiliation.
notes.tip: Keep Danzig (Free City, League), Memel (Allied control) and the Saar (League rule, French mines) apart, and do not mix up Article 231 (war guilt) with Article 227 (trial of the Kaiser).

notes.h: The Treaty of Versailles: colonies, disarmament, reparations and reaction
notes.b: The rest of the treaty stripped Germany of its colonies, its military strength and its wealth. It was also imposed, which explains the German reaction.
points: All Germany's colonies were taken and made League mandates (territories run by a victor state on the League's behalf), held by Britain, France, Japan, Belgium, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

Disarmament, so that Germany could not attack again: the army was limited to 100,000 long-service volunteers, conscription was banned, and there were to be no tanks, military aircraft or submarines. The navy was limited to six battleships and small craft, and the General Staff was abolished.
The Rhineland was demilitarised (the left bank and a 50 km zone on the right bank), and the Allies occupied the left bank for up to fifteen years, to give France security.
Union of Germany and Austria (Anschluss) was forbidden without the consent of the League Council (Article 80).

Reparations (payments for war damage): no total was set in the treaty. Germany was to pay 20 billion gold marks by May 1921 as an interim payment. In May 1921 the London Schedule fixed 132 billion gold marks in A, B and C bonds.
The C bonds (about 82 billion) were not expected to be paid, so the real obligation was about 50 billion.
Article 227 called for the trial of the Kaiser, but the Netherlands refused to hand him over. Part I of the treaty was the Covenant of the League of Nations.

Germans called it a 'Diktat' (a dictated peace) because they had not been allowed to negotiate. Scheidemann's government resigned on 20 June 1919 rather than sign; the Assembly voted to sign on 23 June under the threat of invasion. Hermann Müller and Johannes Bell signed.
notes.tip: Group the terms as territory, colonies, military, reparations and Article 231, then explain why Germans called the treaty a Diktat. Do not say that 132 billion was set at Versailles; it was fixed in 1921.

notes.b: Versailles dealt only with Germany. Separate treaties dealt with Germany's allies, and together they redrew the map of central and south-eastern Europe and the Middle East.
points: The Treaty of St Germain with Austria (10 September 1919) recognised the new states, limited Austria's army to 30,000 and forbade union with Germany. Austria lost South Tyrol to Italy, the Sudeten German areas to Czechoslovakia and Galicia to Poland.

The Treaty of Trianon with Hungary (4 June 1920) cost Hungary about two-thirds of its territory: Transylvania to Romania, Slovakia (and Ruthenia) to Czechoslovakia, Croatia to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and Burgenland to Austria.
Over three million Hungarians were left outside Hungary, which caused bitter and lasting resentment.
The Treaty of Neuilly with Bulgaria (27 November 1919) gave Western Thrace to Greece, which cut Bulgaria off from the Aegean. It also imposed reparations and limited the army to 20,000.

The Treaty of Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire (10 August 1920) divided up the empire, with Armenia and a Kurdish area promised. Mustafa Kemal's nationalists rejected it and defeated Greece (the Greek-Turkish war, 1919-22), and the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) replaced it.
In the Middle East, mandates were allocated at the San Remo conference (April 1920). Britain received Palestine (including Transjordan) and Iraq; France received Syria and Lebanon.
notes.tip: Learn which treaty went with which country: St Germain with Austria, Trianon with Hungary, Neuilly with Bulgaria, Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire, and Lausanne in 1923 with Turkey. Versailles was with Germany only.

notes.b: Self-determination is the principle that peoples should choose the state they belong to. Wilson used it as a guide at Paris, but it was applied in some places and not others, which is why the settlement was criticised.
points: Applied: the settlement created or restored Poland, Czechoslovakia and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which broke away from the Russian Empire in 1917-18, became independent.

Plebiscites in contested areas: Schleswig (1920: the north voted for Denmark, the middle zone for Germany), Allenstein and Marienwerder (July 1920: large majorities for Germany), and Carinthia (October 1920: voted to stay in Austria).
Upper Silesia voted in March 1921 with a majority for Germany, followed by a Polish rising. The League partitioned it in October 1921, giving Poland most of the industrial area.

Denied to Germans: union of Germany and Austria was forbidden although Austria's assembly had voted for it in November 1918. About three million Germans (the Sudeten Germans) were placed in Czechoslovakia, and Germans lived in the Corridor and Danzig.
Denied elsewhere: German-speaking South Tyrol went to Italy to give it a strategic frontier on the Brenner, and Hungarians were left in Romania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia without a choice.

The new states were multinational. Poland had large Ukrainian, Jewish, Belarusian and German minorities, and Czechoslovakia large German and Hungarian minorities. Minority treaties, starting with Poland on 28 June 1919, protected them under League guarantee.
The principle was not applied to the colonies, which became mandates, nor to Ireland, Egypt or India, a fact nationalists there noted.
It could not be applied fully because populations were mixed, states needed ports, railways and defensible frontiers, the victors had their own interests, and wartime promises had been made.
notes.tip: Know cases where it was applied (the new states, plebiscites) and cases where it was denied (Anschluss, Sudetenland, South Tyrol, Hungarians, colonies, Ireland), and explain why it could not be applied fully.

notes.h: The League of Nations and the US Senate
notes.b: Wilson's central aim was a League that would keep the peace. It was created, but the country whose president had invented it refused to join, which weakened it from the start.
points: The League of Nations came into force on 10 January 1920, with its seat in Geneva. Its main organs were the Assembly, the Council and the Secretariat. It also had the Permanent Court of International Justice (The Hague) and the International Labour Organisation (1919).

Its Covenant promised collective security, meaning states acting together against an aggressor. Members were to respect and preserve each other's territorial integrity and political independence (Article 10) and to settle disputes by arbitration.

Under Article 16 members applied economic sanctions, and possibly force, against a member that went to war in breach of the Covenant, so aggression was meant to be deterred by the threat of joint action.
Germany and Soviet Russia were excluded at first. Germany joined in 1926 and the USSR in 1934.

Republicans won control of Congress in the November 1918 elections. The treaty needed a two-thirds majority in the Senate, and the Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Henry Cabot Lodge, proposed reservations, chiefly to Article 10, which could oblige the USA to defend other states.

Wilson refused to compromise. He toured the USA in September 1919 to rally support, collapsed at Pueblo, Colorado, on 25 September and had a stroke on 2 October 1919. The Senate rejected the treaty on 19 November 1919 and again on 19 March 1920.
The USA never joined the League and made a separate peace with Germany (the Treaty of Berlin, August 1921). The Anglo-American guarantee of France lapsed when the Senate did not ratify it.
Without the USA, the strongest Western power, France and Britain were left to enforce the settlement alone.
notes.tip: Give the Senate fight in order: Republican gains in November 1918, Lodge's reservations on Article 10, Wilson's refusal to compromise, the tour and stroke, then rejection in November 1919 and March 1920.

notes.b: Woodrow Wilson was President of the USA from 1913 to 1921. He moved from neutral mediator to war leader to peacemaker, and his Fourteen Points and the League shaped the settlement, but he could not win American support for it at home.
points: Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia. A historian and political scientist, he was President of Princeton University (1902-10) and Governor of New Jersey (1911-13), then Democratic President from 1912 (in office 1913-21). He won the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize.

He kept the USA neutral from 1914, even after the Lusitania was sunk on 7 May 1915 (128 Americans died), and in January 1917 called for 'peace without victory'. He was re-elected in November 1916 on the slogan 'He kept us out of war'.

Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, and the Zimmermann Telegram (a German offer to help Mexico regain lost US territory) was published on 1 March. So on 2 April Wilson told Congress that 'the world must be made safe for democracy'; war came on 6 April.

He announced the Fourteen Points in January 1918 and in February said that self-determination was 'not a mere phrase'. The USA fought as an 'associated power', not a formal ally. He pressed for the Kaiser's removal in the armistice exchanges, so he was a participant, not a witness.

In Paris he was welcomed by huge crowds in December 1918 and January 1919, chaired the commission that drafted the League Covenant and insisted it be in the treaty. To win the League and mandates he compromised on reparations, Article 231, the Saar, the Rhineland, Shandong and South Tyrol.

At home he lost control: Republicans won Congress in November 1918, and he refused Lodge's reservations. His tour ended in a stroke in October 1919, after which his wife Edith controlled access to him, and the Senate rejected the treaty. He died on 3 February 1924.

Contemporary views: Europeans hailed him as a prophet of a new order, while Clemenceau and others were sceptical of his idealism. Keynes portrayed him as outmanoeuvred, and Germans felt disillusioned. Many Americans felt he had entangled the USA in Europe, and nationalists in Ireland and Egypt were disappointed.

Historians: admirers see the founder of liberal internationalism, whose League foreshadowed the United Nations. Critics find him self-righteous, inconsistent on self-determination and politically inept with the Senate, so he was both architect and casualty of the settlement.
notes.tip: Give an accurate sequence with dates: neutrality, the 1916 re-election, entry in April 1917 and its two causes, the Fourteen Points, the armistice, Paris, compromises, the Senate and the stroke. Higher answers must judge his impact: decisive in ending the war and shaping the treaty and League, against failure at home and inconsistency on self-determination.

notes.h: Problems facing Europe after the war
notes.b: The peace did not end Europe's troubles. The war and the treaties left problems that can be grouped as human, economic, political and territorial, each linked to the war or the settlement.
points: Human cost: about 9-10 million soldiers were killed (estimates vary), and millions were wounded and disabled, leaving widows and orphans. The 1918-19 influenza pandemic killed tens of millions worldwide.
Refugees and minorities: the new borders and the break-up of empires left many people living in states ruled by another nationality, or moving across frontiers.

Economic dislocation: governments owed war debts, inflation hurt savings, regions of France and Belgium were damaged, and trade links between the successor states (the new states that replaced the old empires) were broken. The reparations dispute made matters worse.

Political instability: fear of Bolshevism was real, because Soviet republics appeared in Bavaria and Hungary in 1919 and there were risings in Germany. The new democracies were fragile, and the Kapp Putsch showed that the right also threatened them.

Disputed borders led to wars: the Polish-Soviet war of 1919-21 (the battle of Warsaw in August 1920 and the Treaty of Riga in 1921), the Russian Civil War of 1918-21, the Greek-Turkish war, and d'Annunzio's seizure of Fiume with volunteers in September 1919.

Revisionist states, which wanted the treaties revised (Germany, Hungary, Bulgaria and Italy, a disappointed victor), faced status quo states that wanted them kept (France and the new states). This division weakened the peace.
notes.tip: Group the problems as human, economic, political and territorial, link each to the war or the treaties, and finish with a conclusion on which was most serious.

notes.h: Assessment: the German revolution and the Peace Settlement
notes.b: Historians and examiners judge both the German revolution and the Peace Settlement by weighing what they achieved against what they failed to do. The key to a top answer is pairing each achievement with a limit and reaching a conclusion.
points: Revolution, achievement: Germany became a democratic republic with the women's vote and the eight-hour day, and the revolution avoided a Bolshevik-style regime.
Revolution, limit: the old elites in the army, civil service and judiciary were kept, the left was split and embittered by the Freikorps killings, and the republic was tied to defeat and Versailles.

Settlement, achievement: new national states appeared where empires had ruled, and the League provided a forum for settling disputes, such as the Aaland Islands (Finland and Sweden) in 1921. Germany was disarmed but kept as a united state.
Settlement, limit: the new states contained large minorities, and revision was demanded by Germany, Hungary, Bulgaria and Italy, who felt cheated.

The core judgement: the treaty was too harsh to be accepted by Germany but not harsh enough to stop it recovering. Enforcement was left to Britain and France, who disagreed, while the USA and Russia were outside the system.

Contemporary view: Keynes, a Treasury adviser in the British delegation who resigned in June 1919, argued in The Economic Consequences of the Peace (December 1919) that the reparations were unrealistic and would ruin recovery. Foch is credited with saying: 'This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years.'
Germans, for their part, resented the Diktat and the war guilt clause, so the treaty gave nationalists a grievance to exploit.

Later view: some historians say Germany's grievance was exaggerated and its terms were milder than Brest-Litovsk. Others, such as Margaret MacMillan in Peacemakers (2001), see a serious attempt at a difficult task and argue that later failures, not the treaty itself, led to the Second World War.
notes.tip: Use paired points (too harsh against too lenient; achievements against limits of the League; Keynes and Foch against later historians) and finish with a stated conclusion.

keyTerms.definition: The principle, promoted by Wilson, that peoples should choose their own governments and frontiers, usually on national lines; it was applied unevenly in 1919-20.
The principle, in Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, that Germany and its allies were responsible for the war and for all loss and damage, justifying reparations.
Payments imposed on Germany to compensate the Allies; the total was set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921.
The international organisation, founded on 10 January 1920 and based in Geneva, to preserve peace through collective security.
Wilson's statement of war aims and peace principles to Congress on 8 January 1918, which formed the basis for the armistice.
A dictated peace; the German term for the Treaty of Versailles, which Germany was not allowed to negotiate.
A territory taken from Germany or the Ottoman Empire and governed by a victorious power on behalf of the League of Nations.
Volunteer units of ex-soldiers who fought left-wing risings in Germany in 1919 and murdered Luxemburg and Liebknecht.
The nationalist myth that the German army was undefeated in the field and was betrayed by politicians and revolutionaries at home.

factCards.term: Who became German Chancellor on 3 October 1918?

factCards.term: How did the revolution begin in November 1918?
factCards.definition: Sailors refused orders to sail for a last battle; the mutiny at Kiel (from 3 November) spread, and the Kaiser's abdication was announced on 9 November.

factCards.term: Who proclaimed a republic on 9 November 1918?
factCards.definition: Philipp Scheidemann from the Reichstag; Ebert became Chancellor the same day.
A 10 November 1918 deal in which the army promised to support the government in return for help to keep order.
5-12 January 1919 in Berlin; crushed by Freikorps, and Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered on 15 January.

factCards.term: Where did the National Assembly meet in 1919, and why?
factCards.definition: At Weimar, away from the unrest in Berlin; the constitution was adopted in August 1919.

factCards.term: Who were the Big Four at Paris?
factCards.definition: Wilson (USA), Lloyd George (Britain), Clemenceau (France) and Orlando (Italy).
Army of 100,000, no conscription, tanks, air force or submarines, and a demilitarised Rhineland.
Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor, Danzig a Free City, the Saar under the League, and all colonies taken as mandates.
The Reparations Commission fixed the total at 132 billion gold marks.
Reduced Hungary to about a third of its former territory and left over three million Hungarians outside its borders.

factCards.term: Treaties of St Germain, Neuilly, Sèvres
factCards.definition: St Germain (1919) with Austria, Neuilly (1919) with Bulgaria, Sèvres (1920) with the Ottoman Empire.
A general association of nations to guarantee the independence and territorial integrity of all states, which became the League.

factCards.term: Why did the US Senate reject the treaty?
factCards.definition: Republicans led by Lodge feared Article 10 of the Covenant would commit the USA to defend other states; rejected in November 1919 and March 1920.

factCards.term: What was Keynes's criticism of the settlement?
factCards.definition: In The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) he argued that the reparations were unrealistic and would ruin European recovery.
